title: Keep the door open (6:3)
hookLine: like Pharaoh, a person can close the door of return through repeated wrong
tomorrow: is it enough to fix what you did, or also who you are?

lines: A DOOR THAT ISN'T USED STICKS.
A KING WHO KEPT SAYING NO.
cards: A door that isn't used starts to stick. Paint seals the edge, the hinge stiffens, and one day it takes a shoulder to move it. Can a door close so long it won't open again?
Maimonides answers with the hardest case he can find, a king who kept saying no.

teach.b: In chapter six he writes that a person can do wrong so greatly, or so often, that return is withheld from them, and they aren't given the room to turn. His example is Pharaoh.
The Torah says, "I will harden Pharaoh's heart."
Maimonides reads it this way: Pharaoh did wrong first, on his own, again and again, and the hardening came at the end of that road, not at the beginning.
It's a warning about how habits set, not a verdict on anyone listening.
And the same book insists, earlier, that nothing stands in the way of a real return. So the lesson is practical. The door opens most easily while it's still in use.
Look back at this week. Even after death. One deed tips the world.
Wake up, sleepers. Clear the path. Free to choose.

teach.h: A WEEK OF USING THE DOOR.
teach.b: Each one is a way of using the door: naming a wrong, doing one deed, waking up, clearing the floor, choosing on purpose.

how: Jewish teaching on return stresses turning while turning is still easy; the Pharaoh passages of Exodus are read in synagogue each year, and Maimonides' reading of the hardened heart is a classic text on habit and choice.

games.q: what does “keep the door open” mean?
o: welcome every guest who comes to your home
never end a friendship, whatever happens
turn back before repeated wrongs make it hard

p: did wrong first, on his own
at the end of the road, not the start

s: Pharaoh never had a choice; his heart was hardened from the start
Maimonides: Pharaoh did wrong first, on his own, and the hardening came at the end of that road.
Maimonides says repeated wrong can leave a person without room to turn
in chapter six: return can be withheld, as with Pharaoh.
this means some people listening are already beyond return
it's a warning about habits setting; the same book says nothing stands in the way of a real return.

games.q: for months you've told yourself you'll apologize to an old friend 'later.' what does 6:3 point to?
o: now: the door opens most easily while it's still in use.
later is fine; the door of return never gets any harder.
don't bother; after this long, that door is already shut.
games.why: Maimonides warns that a wrong repeated, or a turn put off, makes the way back stiffer. and nothing stands in the way of a real return, so turn now.

practice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms open and facing up, the posture of a door left ajar. Bring to mind one relationship or habit where the hinge has started to stiffen. Keep your hands open, and stay with it until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Keep the door open: Maimonides' warning from Pharaoh. Repeated wrong can close the way back, so turn while turning is still easy.

orig.note: Hebrew: Pharaoh, Maimonides' example of a heart hardened by its own choices.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: keep the door open, because a door in use doesn't stick. Two weeks of return, and more ahead.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 6:3 (return withheld after great or repeated wrong; Pharaoh)
Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 3:14 (nothing stands before return)
